content: The authors propose that it is unlikely that a significant amount of disease went undetected in the study. In an analysis of the WIHS cohort, which included 420 women living with HIV (WLHIV) and 279 HIV-negative women who were cytologically normal and high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) negative at enrollment, the 5-year cumulative incidence rates of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+) were not significantly different between the two groups. Specifically, the rates were 3% in HIV-negative women and 7% (95% CI, 0%-2%) in WLHIV. No cancers were observed in either group. In a separate analysis, WLHIV with CD4+ counts below 500 cells/μL had a higher risk of developing HSIL+ at 39 months compared to those with CD4+ counts above 500 cells/μL. The risk was stratified as follows: 20%-50% for CD4+ counts between 200-500 cells/μL and 9% for CD4+ counts below 200 cells/μL. The same cohort of 1,021 WLHIV and 518 HIV-negative women with normal Pap results at baseline was followed over a median of 5 years (1994-2002) to assess the incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+) and grade 3 or higher (CIN3+). Among women with normal baseline Pap tests and HR-HPV-negative status (n=867), the 5-year cumulative risk of CIN2+ was 2%, 4%, 3%, and 2% in WLHIV with CD4+ counts <350, 350–499, ≥500 cells/μL, and HIV-negative women, respectively. No CIN3+ cases were identified in HIV-negative women, while the cumulative risk of CIN3+ in WLHIV was ≤1% across all CD4+ strata. For women with normal baseline Pap tests but HR-HPV-positive status, the 5-year cumulative risk of CIN2+ was 22%, 12%, 14%, and 10% among WLHIV with CD4+ counts <350, 350–499, ≥500 cells/μL, and HIV-negative women, respectively. The 5-year cumulative risk of CIN3+ was 7%, 2%, and 2% in WLHIV with CD4+ counts <350, 350–499, and ≥500 cells/μL, respectively. WLHIV with normal Pap results who were HPV16-positive had a 5-year cumulative risk of CIN2+ of 29% (95% CI, 6%-46%) and a CIN3+ risk of 10% (95% CI, 0%-23%). WLHIV with non-HPV16 HR-HPV had a 5-year cumulative incidence of 14% (95% CI, 7%-21%) for CIN2+ and 3% (95% CI, 0%-6%) for CIN3+. In a recent update of the cohort, which included women enrolled up to 2015, the 5-year cumulative incidence of precancer (CIN3+ or CIN2+ concurrent with cytologic HSIL) following an HR-HPV-negative test at baseline was 3% (95% CI, 0%-7%), 2% (95% CI, 0%-7%), 1% (95% CI, 0%-3%), and 4% (95% CI, 0%-7%) in WLHIV with CD4+ counts <350, 350–499, ≥500 cells/μL, and HIV-negative women, respectively. No cancers were detected in any group. Three prospective studies evaluated histology-verified CIN2+ incidence in WLHIV with baseline negative visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), HPV-DNA, or cytology tests. In Johannesburg, South Africa, 688 WLHIV without histology-verified CIN2+ at baseline (95% on ART, 90% virally suppressed) were followed for 12 months. The incidence of CIN2+ was 5% in women who were screen-negative with VIA, HR-HPV (Hybrid Capture II), and cytology (<ASCUS). In another study, the incidence of CIN2+ was 2% in WLHIV and HIV-negative women, respectively, over 16 months. A randomized controlled trial in Kenya among 400 WLHIV with CIN2/3 compared cryotherapy and loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). Over 2 years, CIN2+ recurrence was higher in the cryotherapy group (30%) compared to the LEEP group (6%). No studies reported on the risk of treatment failure in HIV-infected women after thermal ablation. Positive surgical margins were associated with higher treatment failure rates (49% vs. 7% for negative margins). The evidence base is limited in WLHIV, and the high persistence of multiple HPV infections makes it challenging to distinguish between treatment failure, recurrence of the original lesion, and the development of new lesions due to different HPV infections. CIN2/3 recurrence may depend on HPV type or variant and its persistence. HPV-DNA-based testing may be useful as a test of cure, as WLHIV with negative HR-HPV tests are likely to be disease-free (NPV = 91%-96%). If negative for both HPV-DNA and cytology, the NPV increases to 99%. However, half of WLHIV testing positive at 6 months did not have recurrent disease, suggesting the need for a second test to rule out recurrence.
